Operations Overview

Are orders fulfilling well?

The 10-second answer, then the evidence behind it.

95.6% of 1,403 orders dispatched within 48 hours across three weeks in Oct 2026 — the final week reached 97.5%, up 3.6pp on the week before, and stock shortages, not processing speed, drove most late orders.

Period: 12 Oct – 1 Nov 2026 · Coverage: 1,403 AU/NZ orders · Grain: one row = one order · Source: weekly fulfilment-rate reports. Definitions on the Data & Definitions tab.

Dispatch within 48h rose in the final week — 94.6% → 93.9% → 97.5%

Takeaway: The dip in week 2 (93.9%) reversed in week 3 (97.5%, +3.6pp) even as volume jumped to 565 orders — the busiest week was also the most reliable. Axis runs 90–100% to show the change; every value is labelled.

Late orders by reason — week of 12–18 Oct only (n = 22)

Takeaway: Stock caused 18 of the 22 late orders that week. Exact reason counts exist only for this week — stock was the dominant reason in all three weeks, but weeks 2–3 reasons are qualitative only, so no counts are shown for them.

So what

Late orders were mostly a stock problem, not a speed problem: in the one week with a full reason breakdown, 18 of 22 late orders were stock-related. That points at stock cover and address checks before dispatch, not at pushing orders faster.

Automation teaser: the repetitive Cin7 order-push step was automated and now runs about 2 rounds a day — with an estimated 60–70% reduction in processing time (Estimated, not measured). How it was built, and what was actually measured, is on Tab 4.

Order to delivery, in four steps

1 · Order intake

Orders land from the Costco portal (Colladium), Shopify stores and Amazon, and are checked for quantity, stock and address problems.

2 · Processing

Orders are registered and pushed in Cin7. This repetitive push step is the one the Python automation took over (see tab 4).

3 · Warehouse & 3PL

Released orders flow to CartonCloud for picking and dispatch from the Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane warehouse.

4 · Tracking & delivery

Consignments are tracked through EWE, AusPost and DHL until delivery; exceptions come back as inquiries (see tab 5).

Sources: Weekly fulfilment-rate reports, 12 Oct – 1 Nov 2026 (411 / 427 / 565 orders checked; 22 / 26 / 14 late). In-transit and handover-week figures as noted on the cards. Sources & definitions →

Logistics Deep Dive

Where do orders get stuck, and why?

Follow the pipeline: not yet shipped → in transit → delivered or late. The blockage sits at the start, not on the road.

Takeaway: Freight is where small errors get expensive: one damaged carton, one wrong warehouse, one short delivery — each one becomes a claim, a return or a re-dispatch.

A

Not yet shipped — most delays start before dispatch

One corrected Costco order shows the whole job — quantity 10 → 6

A Costco purchase order arrived for 10 units of the H60 via the Costco portal (Colladium). After checking, the quantity was corrected from 10 down to 6 before the order was released. A separate cancelled Costco order was voided in Cin7, which released its stock back for the H60 — the correction and the cancellation are two separate events, with no verified link between them and this purchase order.

Takeaway: Catching a 4-unit overstatement before release stops the warehouse picking stock that was never really ordered.

Freight coverage: air, sea and road

  • Air & sea freight — tracked in a dedicated Air Sea Freight Tracking workbook. Inbound sea freight figures are shown below. No freight rates are shown.
  • Road freight — cross-state freight to WA / Perth. Road note from the work: dispatching from Melbourne was faster and cheaper than from Brisbane for that lane.
  • Warehouse choice is a freight decision: the Cin7 push flow picks the warehouse by state and bin stock before anything is released (tab 4).

Takeaway: Picking the right dispatch warehouse is the cheapest freight saving there is — it costs nothing and shortens the longest lane.

Scenario — Projected, not measured

What-if (Scenario): automation coverage vs processing time saved

One decision: if the automation covered a different share of orders, how much processing time would be saved? Drag the slider — Base and Scenario update side by side.

100%
Formula: Time saved = coverage × 65%. 65% is the midpoint of the estimated 60–70% reduction in order-processing time — an estimate, not a measured figure.
Assumptions: the reduction applies uniformly to every order the automation covers; order volume and order mix are unchanged.
Threshold (modelled arithmetic): halving processing time needs about 77% coverage at the 65% midpoint (50 ÷ 65).

Cin7 Order Push

How I cut the manual work

The Cin7 order-push flow for the Shopify Roborock-Store channel — the automation from tab 3, shown step by step.

Takeaway: The automation is conservative by design: it cleans, filters and checks first, pushes second, and stops the whole round if any stage fails.

Channel

Shopify

Roborock-Store channel.

Trigger

Cin7 login

A round starts from a signed-in Cin7 session.

Rounds

~2 per day

Order-push rounds run about twice a day. Counted, not estimated.

Before → after: the same push, no longer by hand

Before — by hand

Each order was registered and pushed by hand in Cin7, one by one. That repetitive push step was the manual work the automation took over.

No count of manual steps eliminated is claimed here: the verified facts are only that orders were registered and pushed by hand, and that the automation took over that repetitive push step.

→

After — automated, checked at every stage

1 Cleanse→2 Filter→2 Warehouse→3 Push→4.5 Restock sweep→5 Report

A local Codex skill + Python program runs the seven stages below. If any stage fails, the round stops — it does not skip ahead. Returns work is analysis only: the automation pushes orders, it never automates returns.

Baseline & Measurement — what was measured, and what was not

ItemStatusWhat the record actually says
Late-order countsMeasuredCounted in the weekly fulfilment-rate reports: 22 / 26 / 14 late orders across 12 Oct – 1 Nov 2026 (see Tab 1).
Push roundsMeasuredOrder-push rounds run about 2 per day.
Real Data aggregatesMeasuredAggregated counts from the working spreadsheets, read 24 Nov 2026 (see Tab 5).
Minutes per order, before vs afterNot measuredProcessing time per order was never timed. No before/after minutes exist.
Error rate before automationNot measuredError rate was not tracked before automation, so no before/after error comparison can be made.
60–70% processing-time reductionEstimatedA revised estimate for the automated order-pushing step — not a measured figure. The What-if model (Tab 3) is built from this estimate.

Takeaway: The gaps are stated plainly on purpose — filling them with invented timings would make the saving look stronger and the work look weaker.

The seven stages

Stage 1 — Cleanse

Incoming orders are cleaned first: duplicates, malformed lines and obvious errors are removed before anything else happens, so later stages only ever see valid orders.

Stage 2 — Filter, branch to Head Office

Orders are filtered to the Roborock-Store channel and branched to Head Office, so store and head-office orders never mix in one push.

Stage 2 (warehouse) — Warehouse selection
  • Only bins with stock on hand greater than 2 are eligible.
  • State priority: NSW / ACT → Sydney first; VIC / TAS / SA / NT → Melbourne first; QLD → Brisbane first.
  • The WA warehouse is not in the automatic rotation.
Stage 3 — Push
  • Stage set to Release To Pick – WMS; invoice date set to today.
  • Saved to Admin, then read back to verify the push actually landed as intended.
Stage 4.5 — Restock sweep

After the main push, a sweep re-checks waiting orders in FIFO order. Only single-item orders are eligible for the sweep, so a restock never half-fills a multi-item order.

Stage 5 — Report

Each round produces a PDF report and an index, and sends a notification — the audit trail for what was pushed, where, and when.

Guardrails — what the automation will never do
  • Runs in DRY-RUN mode for checks before a live push.
  • 3PL setting stays Do Not Transfer to 3PL.
  • Bin stock rule: SOH must be > 2.
  • Passwords are never read or typed by the program; there is no Cin7 API key.
  • If any stage fails, the round stops — it does not skip ahead.

Trade-offs — what was given up, and what still needs a human

  • No API key: the program works through a signed-in Cin7 session, so a round cannot run unattended without one.
  • 3PL stays manual: the 3PL setting is locked to Do Not Transfer to 3PL — transfer decisions stay with a person.
  • WA excluded: the WA warehouse is outside the automatic rotation, so WA orders still need manual handling.
  • Single-item sweep only: the restock sweep never half-fills a multi-item order — safer, but slower to clear waiting multi-item orders.
  • Exceptions stay manual: Costco RA, shortages, PO errors, cross-state transfers, invoice reissue and returns (tab 2) are judgement work the automation does not touch.

What I would improve next — planned, not built yet

  • Automatic retry for a single failed stage, instead of stopping the whole round.
  • An alert when a round stops, so a failure is noticed the same day rather than at the next round.
  • A timed before/after measurement of minutes per order, so the 60–70% estimate can be replaced with a measured figure.
  • Error tracking before and after automation, so an error-rate comparison becomes possible.

Takeaway: None of these four is done — they are the next steps, listed so the current state is not overstated.

Role scope: the local Codex skill + Python program that runs the push was built for this role. Cin7, Shopify, CartonCloud and the carrier systems are the company's systems — used and configured here, not built here.

Automation & handover

The project was handed over in three steps:

1 · Transfer the project

The program and its project files were passed to the team taking over the work.

2 · Restore and verify

The setup was restored on the other side and checked against a live round before sign-off.

3 · Account and tool portability

Notes covered what depends on accounts or tools, so the workflow does not silently depend on one person's login.

Takeaway: Automation only counts as finished when someone else can run it — the handover is part of the result.

Execution loop

Each round runs the same fixed loop from start (R) to finish (Z), so every round is checked the same way and any failure is easy to locate.

Data & Definitions

Can I trust these numbers?

Appendix: every figure on the other four tabs traces back to a source below. Aggregated counts from the 360 working Google Sheets, read on 24 Nov 2026. Aggregates only: no customer names, addresses, contact details or individual order numbers appear anywhere in this section.

Takeaway: The real sheets tell the same story as the first four tabs — a high-volume operation where address changes, deliveries in flight and returns are the daily workload, and most of it closes out.

Reconciliation — the sums check out: inquiries 153 completed + 70 in progress + 31 pending = 254; return outcomes 186 + 277 + 31 + 13 + 9 + 165 = 681; in-transit channels 69 + 44 + 5 + 2 + 15 = 135; Hohem carriers 23 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 34. One sum that does not reconcile, explained: the Open list (53) + Closed list (103) = 156, not 254 — the “total sheet” is a consolidated tracker that merges several lists (Inquiries 127, completed list 37, Cin7 new registrations 28, merged multi-source items 12, 50 with no source label), so the live lists and the tracker count different things.

What cannot be computed — gaps stated, not filled

MeasureWhy it is missing
On-time-in-full (OTIF) %No in-full / complete-order data was recorded, so OTIF cannot be computed. Dispatch within 48h (Tab 1) is a timing measure only — it says nothing about completeness.
Cost per orderCost data exists only in the Aug–Oct 2024 freight sheets; none was recorded for 2025–2026. No proxy is used in its place.
Average days lateDays late per order was not recorded — only whether an order exceeded 48h.
Minutes per order, before vs after automationProcessing time per order was never timed. The 60–70% reduction is an estimate, not a measurement.
Error rate before automationErrors were not tracked before automation, so no before/after error comparison exists.
A delivery target (e.g. 95%)No delivery target was stated for this operation. None is invented here, and no chart on this dashboard is drawn against a target line.

Known holes in the underlying data: the Air Sea Freight Tracking workbook was read on 25 Nov 2026 (downloaded copy, read-only); inbound freight figures are on Tab 2; stock-on-hand and incoming-stock figures were not available (login-gated files), so no stock-cover figures are shown; the Delivered tab's product split is not shown because its columns shift between rows; 54 in-transit orders carry no booking date and are excluded from the by-month chart; the inquiries WATCH LIST (570 rows, Nov 2025 – Mar 2026, mostly no status) is historical only and is not charted.
